title: Fundamentals of Cognitive Science
objectives: This course introduces the foundations of neuroscience and cognitive neuroscience from cellular and biophysical mechanisms to systems and cognition. Students learn how neurons generate and transmit electrical signals, how synapses and neurotransmitters support communication in neural circuits, and how major sensory, motor, memory, and attention systems are organized. The course also develops a quantitative understanding of neural function through computational neuron models and psychophysical methods, enabling students to connect biological mechanisms with perception, behavior, and cognition.
syllabus:
1. Foundations of Cognitive Science and Functional Neuroanatomy: Introduction to cognitive neuroscience, cognitive science, and levels of analysis; historical development and localization of brain function; functional neuroanatomy: central and peripheral nervous systems, cerebral cortex, subcortical structures, and brain organization.
2. Cellular and Molecular Neurobiology: Neurons and glial cells; cellular structure, organelles, cytoskeleton, and myelination; neuronal membrane, ion channels, ion selectivity, electrochemical gradients, and resting membrane potential.
3. Biophysics of Excitable Membranes and Computational Neuron Models: Action potentials, voltage-gated ion channels, propagation of neural signals, and optogenetics; Hodgkin-Huxley model and quantitative analysis of neuronal excitability; integrate-and-fire and leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) computational neuron models.
4. Synaptic Transmission and Neurochemistry: Synaptic transmission: electrical and chemical synapses, presynaptic and postsynaptic mechanisms; neurotransmitters, receptors, transporters, retrograde messengers, second-messenger systems, and protein kinases.
5. Psychophysics and Decision Theory: Psychophysics: absolute and difference thresholds, method of limits, method of constant stimuli, and psychometric functions; Signal Detection Theory, sensitivity, criterion, and perceptual decision-making under uncertainty.
6. Sensory Systems and Perception: Chemical senses: gustation and olfaction; visual system: retinal organization, phototransduction, early visual processing, visual pathways, and cortical processing; auditory system and neural processing of sound; somatosensory system, touch, and body sensation.
7. Motor Systems and Neural Control: Motor system organization, skeletal muscle control, spinal reflexes, and cortical motor control mechanisms.
8. High-Level Cognitive Functions: Learning and memory: hippocampal function, place cells, grid cells, synaptic plasticity, and cellular mechanisms of memory; attention: overt and covert attention, bottom-up and top-down mechanisms, and spatial, feature-based, and object-based attention.
textbooks:
1. Eric R. Kandel, John D. Koester, Sarah H. Mack, and Steven A. Siegelbaum, Principles of Neural Science, 6th Edition, McGraw-Hill.
2. Mark F. Bear, Barry W. Connors, and Michael A. Paradiso, Neuroscience: Exploring the Brain, 4th Edition, Wolters Kluwer.
3. Robert E. Kass, Uri T. Eden, and Emery N. Brown, Analysis of Neural Data, Springer Series in Statistics, Springer.
